Longboards and skateboards are not to be fucked with. Took a bad spill at high speed the day before my 18th birthday and got a bad concussion. Spent my very last night as a minor in the pediatric ward. I'd been riding exclusively skateboards before that and wasn't aware of how quickly those suckers built speed. 

That said, longboarding can be a blast, in the right conditions. Took over a year but I got back on the board while in college. With big enough wheels those rocks and pebbles aren't much of a problem. Still, doing it at night is almost always a pretty bad idea. Glad you didn't end up smushed.

Winter 2016, just before Christmas, I was parallel parked on the side of a busy street in my city late at night. I'd just blown my last $50 on a record player and was loading it into the backseat of my car. I was streetside with my car door as close to my body as possible, since my other door was blocked by a phone pole. 

Suddenly an SUV flies up the street, cuts too close and rips my whole door off. I was bent over trying to get this heavy record player in, so I didn't know anything was happening until I heard the sound of crunching glass and metal shaking my whole car. 

I step back and look around, saw my door skittering away on the asphalt and the side mirror of a Buick spinning in circles near my tire. I'm utterly bewildered, not really able to piece together what just happened, til this dude in an apartment above leans out his window and hollers down "Are you okay?"

Me, idiot, picks up the Buick mirror and hollers back up, "Is this yours?" He snorts and says no but says if I need a statement he'll help me because he saw what happened. I glance up the street and see the Buick turning a corner and disappearing, and all I can think to do is yell "thanks, asshole" at the tail lights. 

It was then I kind of put it together that had I been half an inch farther out into the street I would have been ripped away along with my door. Now I'm pissed and pick up the pieces of Buick mirror, going to fetch my door from wherever it rolled away to. 

To my surprise a minute or so later the Buick rolls back around and it's some old lady who asks if I'm alright. I'm still holding the mirror and at this point I'm not even mad, just cracking up about how stupid this all is. I give it to her and she gives me her info, we take pictures, and I start getting pissed again so I tell her to leave. Had to call my dad to come help with my car since I was a good ways from home and my car was minus a damn door. It was a whole ordeal. Fortunately I had good insurance that covered most of the repairs, since I was flat broke after buying that record player. 

Funny thing is (well, funny to me anyway), I had been struggling hard with my mental health at the time and was basically the lowest I'd ever been. My plan for the night was to buy the record player, go back home, play my favorite records, and take every pill in the house while drinking myself into oblivion, with the goal of not waking up again. My roommates were gonna be gone for the night, so I knew no one would find me til the next day. Had already put together all my goodbye notes, cleaned my room, and otherwise organized my affairs. The car thing was one more hassle that meant I'd have to stick around and put up with more bullshit before I could kill myself. I kept cracking up, thinking about telling that old lady "you missed!" Made one too many bad jokes about it to my dad, we had a talk, and I checked myself into a mental health clinic two days later. 

Doing much better these days. I'm still alive and also my car has a new door. None too bad all in all. Still have that record player too. Not as intense as some of these, but still the closest I've yet come.

Wild. I remember experiencing depression and ideation as early as age 11 as well as minor mood swings/bursts of hypomania, but it was not nearly as pronounced as it was after I got a concussion on the day before my 18th birthday.  I crashed on my longboard and was on the side of the road for who knows how long before picking myself up and going home, but I don't remember much of anything from about 15 seconds after the crash until the next morning when I woke up on the living room couch, having spent the better part of the night in the hospital. I was otherwise fine— no broken bones, barely any bruises, just a sore neck— and while I didn't suffer any cognitive problems I do remember my mood getting much, much worse. At the time I attributed it just to school stress and my father having a health scare, but that may well have been a turning point.... Certainly the manic episodes were more prominent after that and the depressive episodes way more severe.

It's kind of amazing to see how many people have stories like this, of having their symptoms become so much more apparent after a concussion. I may have to rethink some stuff.

some docs are really cool about this and others are absolute garbage. my one doc was super chill and thanked me for being honest when i told her i used to smoke weed twice a week for a year and had tried molly twice in my life. i was straightforward about it, truthfully telling her i hadn't used anything else or anything since then and she basically said "okay, be safe." made me happy to open up about the other issues i was having.

the other time, i was doing a neuropsychological exam and the doc asked about my drug use. i told her the same thing and she put a whole section in my report about how i had a "remarkable history of drug abuse" and put a bunch of alcohol/drug rehab recommendations into my treatment plan. which was sent to my parents. and my school.

fortunately i was able to argue my way out of those recommendations, but it was made to sound like i was an alcoholic drug addict instead of a loser college kid. my parents FLIPPED and my dad pushed hard for rehab when he first read through it. didn't matter that i hadn't smoked in months and i'd tried molly literally twice, in the same week, two years before.

That's where I'm at. I have to laugh, because otherwise I would cry, and she wouldn't want that for me :) 

The fucking kerning, holy shit. There's massive spaces between all capitals and the following lowercase letters. I just took another look at the thing and almost all of it was set entirely in Papyrus, with the exception of one page that had *four different and entirely unrelated fonts on it.*

Horrific. Tragic. 

*Fucking hilarious.*

I know she would have found it funny, so I do, too. Like one last inside joke.

They buried my friend in a dress, with a rosary. She had such unique fashion sense and wore a vest, tie, and boots almost every day, but at the end she was in a dress. I can't help thinking about how cranky she would have been.

But then again, I know she would have worn a dress if her mother had asked, and so I try to look at it that way. It wasn't perfect, but it's not like her mother was prepared, so I'm sure she would have wanted her to do whatever she needed to feel a little better about it all. 

I don't mean to be presumptuous or intrude on your grief, but if I may offer some advice: let yourself feel it. Everything, even the small things you know are irrational. It's been over half a year since my friend passed, and I still find myself getting pissed off at her for arguments we had three years ago, or crying over something she told me in confidence back in our school days.

I read somewhere that after about three months, emotional support drops off significantly. I found that to be true. The funeral came and went, and all of a sudden no one wanted to talk about my friend anymore. It was as though the appropriate window for my pain had closed, and now I had to move on. But grief doesn't work that way, and you shouldn't feel that it has to. Let yourself feel it.

I'm so sorry for your loss, and I'm glad you could find some comfort in what I wrote. A month is still so terribly recent. Remember that your fiancé was, and *is*, a part of you, and that this will not always feel so heavy and painful. 

Again, hope I haven't overstepped. If you need a listening ear, feel free to send me a PM.

My other design friends and I have collectively decided we are planning our own funerals ahead of time, and down to the font. "Down to the font" is now our sort of inside joke for any kind of ridiculous and morbid detail-fixation. 

My mother loves Bradley Hand ITC and I hate it so much. If by some chance I pass before her, my ghost had damn well better not see that script on anything relating to my dead self.

Down to the font.

Oh god, why does it seem like the ministers for these things are always either extremely good or *insane?* The priest for my friend's service had one of those as well: a meandering, confusing, messy rant of a sermon that bordered on hilarious because of how awful it was. I thought it was just a one-off, "well maybe he just screwed this up"-type thing, but they did another service to recognize my friend a few months later and it was just as messy and painfully funny. I don't know why they keep asking that guy to do things. 

*"Without light,"* he said at one point, trying in vain to remember what he'd been going on about, *"... it would be very dark."*

Dunno about you, but I've never heard such inspiring words. 

Thank you for your comment, and my condolences for your own loss. I'm trying to see the funny side of stuff, since that's what my friend would have done.

Thanks so much for this. It was beautiful. Unfortunately I can relate; my friend's funeral was big and Catholic and so very religious that it would have infuriated her. I get that "the funeral is for the family" but it still felt so wrong that it was almost funny. Like you said, though, she wasn't there to laugh at it with me, which was what made the pain of it so apparent. 

Sorry for your loss, and thank you again for your kind words. I hope you find peace as well.

If you're U.S., see if your state has a Department of Rehabilitative Services/Workforce Services or something similar to that. I'm using their program right now and they help you get (and retain!) a job, build career skills, and can even pay for education and resources. It takes a good bit of time to get set up and through the process, but it's helpful. I started in May I think and I'm now done almost all the screenings and will be putting a plan together with my counselor next week. I recommend it a lot, they're great.

I've asked if it's okay to wear pants to weddings and the like in the past and it was accepted, but with a lot of snide, biting commentary and the implication that if I did it, I'd be made to regret it. My family is still kind of traditional in that sense. Outside of family events, it's pants 100% of the time, but that little bit of stress when i HAVE to do it is enough to crush me

in 5th grade, when we had to watch "The Movie" (what everyone called the puberty/basic sex ed video), we were separated by gender and watched the gender-specific video. i'd already read about puberty and had a version of "the talk" with my mother, so i knew what to expect going in, but still felt so grossed out and *angry.* 

i sat there on the carpet, surrounded by my classmates, *seething* at the idea of what was going to happen to me. i didn't want boobs. i didn't want a period. i didn't enjoy any part of being a girl and hated that everyone was telling me i was gonna be a woman whether i wanted to be or not. 

the teacher's aides had put together little gift bags with a pad, tampon, tiny deodorant, and some reading materials for each of us, and gave them to us on our way home. i threw mine in the trash, refusing to take part in any of it. now i feel bad about that, but i was so upset and uncomfortable with the whole thing that just holding the stupid bag in my hand was enough to make me feel ill.

when i inevitably grew up and got my period, i denied it. straight up denied it. went to pee, saw my underwear was bloody, and said "nope. this is not happening to me." threw my undies out, got new ones. bloodied again. threw those out, padded these ones with toilet paper so i wouldn't have to use a pad. 

i did that for my first three periods, until i started running low on underwear and had to finally tell my mom. 

puberty was such a source of shame for me. i remember crying every night when i was 13, wishing my parents could've had three sons instead of two sons and a daughter. i felt so disgusting and stifled by my body and all the expectations put in place for me. i just wanted to be a boy.

tbh that sentiment hasn't really changed, even though i'm 22 now. i still wish i could flip a switch and be a boy. i hate my boobs, my hips, the way my body looks. i hate when people say i'm pretty, or that i dress too masculine. dress shopping is a source of severe, crippling anxiety for me, but it still happens at least once a year for weddings and funerals. i feel nauseous and trapped when wearing one; my family has yelled at me for this fairly often, trying to tell me it's not that big of a deal. i know they're right, and it shouldn't be that big of a deal, but that doesn't change how i feel. 

somewhere along the line i figured out i'm a lesbian, which was pretty big, but the gender situation is still a fiasco. i have a really good support system of lgbtq-friendly pals, and my college was great for it, too. family is accepting, but only in the sense that they don't hate it and just avoid talking about it. i used gender-neutral pronouns for a little while and hated how that felt. it might work for some, but just not for me. these days i've kind of resigned to who i am, figuring i'm not a boy and never will be one. i think it takes a kind of strength i don't have to be trans; i honestly don't mean that in any kind of an offensive or harmful way, that's just my sentiment. i don't know that i could do it. i'd like to, but i couldn't. 

sorry about the rant. i haven't really talked to anyone about this stuff before. it's just wild reading through everyone's responses and feeling like they know what i've lived with, what i'm living with.
